corpus: 9 sites, 795 pages, 4 generators (Yoast, RankMath, SlimSEO, The SEO Framework)
_method: Measurement can only rule properties OUT, never in. A property observed
carrying two values somewhere in the corpus is definitively not functional.
A property never observed multi-valued proves nothing: `image` appears 2,098
times across 7 sites and is never multi-valued here, yet a product gallery
makes it plural, and treating it as functional would manufacture
contradictions on the first site with two photos.
So `basis: observed` entries are empirical and settled. `basis: asserted`
entries are a deliberate policy choice, stricter than RDF allows, made
because a divergence under one @id is a finding worth reporting. That
assertion is the product (see dev-notes/00), not a discovery.
_default: Anything absent from this file is treated as MULTI-VALUED, and therefore
never raises entity.contradiction. Silence is the safe default: the cost of
a missing functional property is one unreported finding, while the cost of a
wrongly-functional property is a false contradiction on every site that uses
it legitimately. The corpus has 122 distinct properties and only 11 are
listed as functional; that ratio is deliberate.
_keys: Keys are full IRIs, because extraction compares post-expansion IRIs rather
than as-written names. Normalise http://schema.org to https://schema.org
before lookup (dev-notes/03) or mixed-vintage markup will miss.
A same-named property in another vocabulary is a different IRI and

https://schema.org/name.note: The most-used property in the corpus and never plural. An entity with two names under one @id is an identity problem.

https://schema.org/url.note: The M0 flagship finding: a corpus site carries two url values under one @id across 150 pages.

https://schema.org/logo.note: Distinct from `image`, which is legitimately plural.

https://schema.org/address.note: A multi-site business would break this. Revisit if one appears in the corpus.

https://schema.org/telephone.note: Stricter than RDF on purpose. A business genuinely can have two numbers, but publishing different ones under one @id on different pages is the flagship contradiction this tool exists to catch.

https://schema.org/legalName.note: A registered legal identity is singular by definition.

https://schema.org/geo.note: Thin evidence, but one entity has one set of coordinates.

https://schema.org/priceRange.note: Thin evidence. Semantically a single band.

https://schema.org/vatID.note: Not observed in the corpus. Singular by definition.

https://schema.org/faxNumber.note: Not observed. Included for symmetry with telephone.

https://schema.org/sameAs.note: Plural 89% of the time. Compare as a set — order is never a finding.

https://schema.org/image.note: Observed plural only once in 2,098, which is exactly why measurement alone is untrustworthy: the semantics are plural regardless of what this corpus happens to contain.

https://schema.org/itemListElement.note: Ordered. Breadcrumb checks care about order; contradiction checks must not.

https://schema.org/contactPoint.note: Never plural in this corpus, but an organisation legitimately has several — sales, support, press. Asserted plural despite the data, which is the mirror image of the telephone case.

https://schema.org/openingHoursSpecifica.note: One entry per day band is the normal shape.

_candidates: Considered and deliberately left non-functional, to be revisited at M1
shakedown against real findings rather than now:
description (1,874 occurrences, never plural) — divergence is far more
likely to be truncation or page context than a genuine contradiction.
headline, datePublished, dateModified — page-scoped, so they rarely have
cross-page observations of one @id, which is when this list applies.
price, sku, brand — product-scoped and worth revisiting once the corpus
contains a store with a real duplicate-product problem.
